title: Yann LeCun
text:
Yann LeCun (born July 8, 1960) is a French-American computer scientist best known as a pioneer of artificial intelligence and deep learning, particularly for inventing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that revolutionized computer vision and pattern recognition. He is Executive Chairman of Advanced Machine Intelligence (AMI Labs) and Silver Professor of Data Science, Computer Science, Neural Science, and Electrical and Computer Engineering at New York University (NYU), affiliated with the Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences and the Center for Data Science.

LeCun received the 2018 ACM A.M. Turing Award, shared with Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, for conceptual and engineering breakthroughs in deep learning.

#Early life and education

#Early life

Yann LeCun was born on July 8, 1960, in Soisy-sous-Montmorency, a suburb of Paris, France. He grew up in the Paris suburbs. His father was an aeronautical engineer with interests in electronics and mechanics, who encouraged hands-on experimentation. LeCun engaged in tinkering with devices during his boyhood.

As a child, LeCun watched Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey at around age nine while living in Paris, noting the intelligent computer HAL 9000. He attended secondary school in the French education system, which emphasized mathematics and physics.

#Education

Yann LeCun earned his Diplôme d'Ingénieur in electrical engineering from ESIEE Paris in 1983.

He then pursued advanced studies at Université Pierre et Marie Curie (now Sorbonne University), obtaining a Diplôme d'Études Approfondies (DEA) in 1984 and a Ph.D. in computer science in 1987. His doctoral thesis, titled Modèles connexionnistes de l'apprentissage, supervised by Maurice Milgram, focused on connectionist models of learning, particularly neural networks applied to pattern recognition tasks.

Following his Ph.D., LeCun conducted postdoctoral research at the University of Toronto from 1987 to 1988 as a research associate in Geoffrey Hinton's group, where he further explored neural network models. This collaboration strengthened his focus on practical implementations of neural networks.

#Professional career

#Bell Labs and AT&T Labs

In 1988, following a postdoctoral fellowship at the University of Toronto, Yann LeCun joined AT&T Bell Laboratories as a member of the technical staff in the Adaptive Systems Research Department, located in Holmdel, New Jersey. There, he applied neural network techniques to practical problems in image processing and pattern recognition.

During the early 1990s at Bell Labs, LeCun led efforts that produced convolutional neural network systems for handwritten digit recognition, deployed in hardware for applications such as reading postal codes on envelopes in collaboration with the United States Postal Service (USPS), processing millions of items daily to automate mail sorting. His team also developed similar systems for optical character recognition (OCR) on bank checks, extracting handwritten amounts and fields to streamline financial processing.

In 1996, following the corporate divestiture that restructured Bell Labs into AT&T Labs-Research, LeCun transitioned to the new entity and was appointed head of the Image Processing Research Department in Red Bank, New Jersey, a position he held until 2002. Under his leadership, the department advanced applied projects in document analysis, including the development of the DjVu image compression format in collaboration with researchers such as Léon Bottou and Patrick Haffner; DjVu enabled efficient storage and transmission of scanned documents by separating text and background layers, achieving compression ratios superior to JPEG for color pages.

As department head, LeCun supervised a team of researchers, fostering collaborations that resulted in over a dozen patents on neural network-based recognition systems and image processing techniques during his tenure at AT&T Labs. His group produced key publications, including the 1998 paper on gradient-based learning applied to document recognition, which demonstrated performance benchmarks for convolutional networks in OCR tasks using datasets from USPS mail and check images. These efforts established early industrial applications of such networks in automating vision tasks.

#NEC Laboratories America

In 2002, Yann LeCun joined NEC Laboratories America in Princeton, New Jersey, as a Fellow, where he served until late 2003. This brief appointment represented a transitional leadership role, bridging his industrial experience at AT&T Labs with impending academic positions, including his move to New York University.

During this period, LeCun's efforts centered on high-level research themes in machine learning applications for multimedia and computer vision, extending his prior expertise in image processing. His work emphasized collaborations, notably with Léon Bottou, on scalable approaches to vision and multimedia tasks amid shifting industrial research priorities following the dot-com era. These partnerships included engagements with academic institutions to facilitate knowledge transfer.

#New York University

In 2003, Yann LeCun joined the Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences at New York University as a Professor of Computer Science, transitioning to full-time academia after industrial research. He was promoted to Silver Professor in 2008, a distinguished title for his contributions. As of 2025, he holds the Jacob T. Schwartz Professorship in the departments of Computer Science and Data Science at the Courant Institute, alongside Silver Professorships in Data Science, Computer Science, Neural Science, and Electrical and Computer Engineering across the university, solidifying his interdisciplinary influence.

LeCun provided key leadership in building NYU's data science programs, directing the university's data science initiative from 2012 to 2014 to enable interdisciplinary artificial intelligence collaboration. In 2013, he founded and directed the NYU Center for Data Science, establishing it as a research and education hub that promoted partnerships across NYU schools and advanced data-driven innovations.

LeCun has shaped NYU's academic programs through teaching and mentoring, developing foundational courses in machine learning, computer vision, and Deep Learning that integrate theory, supervised/unsupervised methods, representation learning, and applications. He co-leads initiatives like "Big Ideas in Artificial Intelligence" for interdisciplinary AI education. In supervision, he guides PhD students advancing deep learning, self-supervised learning, and probabilistic machine learning, including advisees such as Yilun Kuang and Katrina Evtimova, contributing to long-term field development.

#Meta AI Research

In December 2013, Yann LeCun was appointed founding Director of AI Research at Facebook (now Meta), with the lab's headquarters in New York City. He retained a part-time professorship at New York University. Under his leadership, the Fundamental AI Research (FAIR) lab expanded globally, establishing sites in Paris in 2015, followed by Montreal and London. FAIR contributed to open-source tools, including the development of PyTorch, a deep learning framework.

FAIR integrated AI into Meta's platforms for applications such as personalized recommendations and content moderation. The lab developed tools to detect and mitigate biases in AI models. In discussions on AI safety, LeCun has advocated for approaches like objective-driven training to address risks, while expressing concerns about regulations that may impede innovation.

By November 2025, LeCun held the title of Chief AI Scientist at Meta, focusing on long-term AI goals including systems with human-like reasoning capabilities. In November 2025, he announced plans to depart Meta in the coming months to found a startup developing AI systems based on world models.

#Research contributions

#Convolutional neural networks and deep learning

Yann LeCun pioneered convolutional neural networks (CNNs), introducing architectures inspired by the organization of the mammalian visual cortex as described by neuroscientists David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel. These networks employ convolutional layers to detect local features such as edges and textures, utilizing shared weights to enforce translation invariance and reduce parameters compared to fully connected networks, thereby enhancing efficiency for image processing tasks.

CNNs incorporate pooling operations for spatial invariance alongside convolutional layers with shared weights, enabling the capture of local patterns and the learning of hierarchical representations—from low-level features to complex objects—through multi-layer structures trained end-to-end via backpropagation and stochastic gradient descent. These conceptual innovations addressed limitations in prior neural network approaches, establishing CNNs as benchmarks for image recognition tasks by improving scalability and performance in computer vision.

LeCun contributed to the deep learning renaissance by advocating multi-layer neural networks during an era dominated by shallow models and support vector machines, emphasizing scalable training techniques through publications and collaborations. Working with Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio—recognized as pioneers of deep learning—his foundational research on CNNs influenced subsequent advances, including deeper architectures that achieved breakthroughs in large-scale image classification competitions, fostering widespread adoption of deep learning via GPU-accelerated training and hierarchical feature learning.

#Other innovations in machine learning and computer vision

#Software tools

LeCun co-authored the Lush programming language in the 1990s with Léon Bottou, an object-oriented Lisp dialect tailored for rapid prototyping in numerical computing, graphics, and machine learning. This tool facilitated efficient experimentation in artificial intelligence by blending interpreted scripting with compiled efficiency, influencing early development of graph-based AI systems.

At AT&T Labs, LeCun pioneered the DjVu file format in 1996, a wavelet-based compression technology for scanned documents that separated foreground text from background images for compact storage and transmission. DjVu advanced efficient digital document handling, supporting web distribution and laying groundwork for scalable data processing in early machine learning applications.

#Invariant representations and datasets

LeCun advanced computer vision through techniques for learning invariant representations robust to variations in pose, lighting, and clutter. His NORB dataset, featuring stereo images of objects under varied conditions, enabled hierarchical feature learning for object recognition, emphasizing semantic invariances and reducing dependence on data augmentation, which bolstered foundational progress in robust perception systems.

#Energy-based models and self-supervised learning

In 2006, LeCun introduced energy-based models (EBMs), which assign scalar energy scores to data configurations to capture dependencies across supervised, unsupervised, and semi-supervised learning without explicit probability normalization. This unified framework supported predictive learning and self-supervised representations, extending LeCun's influence toward scalable, dependency-focused models.

Building on EBMs, LeCun proposed the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) in 2022, a non-generative self-supervised method that predicts latent representations of masked targets from context via energy minimization. JEPA enabled efficient world model learning from unlabeled video by focusing on abstract predictions rather than pixel reconstruction, with extensions to video (V-JEPA) and vision-language tasks advancing spatiotemporal understanding and robotic planning without exhaustive rendering. These developments highlight LeCun's ongoing emphasis on predictive, non-generative approaches for building intuitive physical world models in AI.
In March 2026, LeCun's team introduced LeWorldModel, a 15M-parameter JEPA that achieves stable training with a simple two-term loss and enables full planning in under one second on one GPU from raw pixel inputs, advancing world model capabilities for AI agents.

#Awards and honors

#Major scientific awards

Yann LeCun has received several awards recognizing his contributions to artificial intelligence, deep learning, and convolutional neural networks.

In 2018, LeCun shared the ACM A.M. Turing Award with Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio for conceptual and engineering breakthroughs establishing deep neural networks as a critical component of computing.

In 2023, LeCun received the Global Swiss AI Award for his impact in artificial intelligence, particularly through advancements in computer vision and machine learning.

In 2024, LeCun received the VinFuture Prize for his development of convolutional neural networks.

In 2025, LeCun was one of seven laureates awarded the Queen Elizabeth Prize for Engineering for advancements in modern machine learning, including artificial neural networks.

Also in 2025, LeCun received the inaugural Trailblazer Award from the New York Academy of Sciences for his work in machine learning, computer vision, mobile robotics, and artificial intelligence.

#Academic and professional distinctions

Yann LeCun has been elected to several prestigious academic academies, recognizing his foundational contributions to artificial intelligence and machine learning. He became a member of the United States National Academy of Engineering in 2017 for developing convolutional neural networks and their applications in computer vision and other areas of artificial intelligence. In 2021, he was elected to the United States National Academy of Sciences, as well as named a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science. He is also a member of the French Académie des Sciences.

LeCun has received numerous honorary doctorates from leading institutions worldwide. These include a Doctor Honoris Causa from the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) in 2018, the Instituto Politécnico Nacional in Mexico City in 2016, Université Côte d'Azur in France in 2022, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology in 2023, Università di Siena in Italy in 2023, and the University of Geneva in Switzerland in 2024.

Among his other honors, LeCun was appointed Chevalier (Knight) in the Ordre national de la Légion d'honneur by the French government in 2020. He has also held editorial positions, including as an associate editor for IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence from 2003 to 2005.

LeCun's influence extends through invited talks at major conferences and advocacy for open-source AI in global forums.
